Every expression has a value category, and since C++17 there are three. An lvalue names an object that already exists, such as a variable. A prvalue, pure rvalue, computes a value or initialises an object and has no object of its own until it needs one, such as
or a call that returns by value. An xvalue, expiring value, refers to an object that already exists but whose resources may be taken, the result of
casts its argument to an xvalue. It moves nothing by itself.

The problem is the copy nobody can read again. Before C++11, a function that returned a large container by value built the result in a temporary, copied it element by element into the caller's variable, and destroyed the temporary, so returning a container of thousands of entries paid for a full copy on the way out, and again on assignment, for a value nothing could see afterwards.
The mechanism is overload resolution reading the source's value category. A copy constructor takes
. An rvalue, a prvalue or an xvalue, binds to

and selects the move constructor, which is free to take the source's internal state, because nothing can look at the source afterwards. Since C++17, when a prvalue initialises an object of the same type, copy elision is guaranteed: the object is built directly, with no copy or move constructor called at all.

You meet this in every container and message the robot's nodes pass between callbacks, and it is the interview question itself: naming the value category of an expression and saying which constructor, if any, runs from it.
